scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Developed during the Viceroyalty of Peru with roots in the Iberian Peninsula, the dance was assimilated by enslaved and free Africans.
Post-independence (1821), communities in Lima's alleyways formed cuadrillas to perform it during Corpus Christi and later Carnival.
Banned by the Church in 1817 and fading mid-20th century, it was revived on stage in 1956 by Estampas de Pancho Fierro and returned to the streets in 1986 by the Movimiento Negro Francisco Congo.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally associated with Corpus Christi and subsequently with Carnival and regional festival dates like San Juan in Cañete.
It serves as an expression of Afro-Peruvian identity, reclaiming public space through theatricality.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Driven by guitars, the cajita (a small wooden box opened and closed for rhythmic accents), and the quijada de burro (a donkey, horse, or mule jawbone hit to create a raspy buzz).
Listen for the Guitar, Cajita, Quijada.
A lively street sound driven by strummed guitars, the crisp percussion of the wooden cajita, and the sharp, raspy rattle of the horse or donkey jawbone (quijada).

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Performers dress as devils, wearing horned masks, tails, and holding tridents, as depicted in 19th-century watercolors by Pancho Fierro.
Set primarily in public streets, plazas, and alleys during carnivals.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Nicomedes Santa Cruz (researcher), Pancho Fierro (19th-century watercolorist), José Durand (revivalist in the 1950s), and the Movimiento Negro Francisco Congo (returned the dance to the streets in 1986).

Practiced historically and currently in Lima and the Cañete Province (such as San Luis de Cañete), sharing thematic traits with the broader Andean Diablada tradition while retaining distinct Afro-Peruvian instrumentation.
Evolved from Spanish colonial and Catholic celebrations combined with Afro-Peruvian performance practices, drawing slight comparative parallels to the Diabladas of Oruro.
